title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is defined as the sudden, unexpected death of an infant younger than 1 year that remains unexplained after a thorough investigation, including review of clinical history, examination of the death scene, and complete autopsy. SIDS represents the leading cause of death among infants aged 1 to 12 months in the United States. It is classified as a subtype of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID), which includes all sudden, unexpected deaths in infancy, whether explained or unexplained. While some SUID cases can be attributed to identifiable causes, a diagnosis of SIDS is assigned only when no cause is determined. Risk factors include prone sleeping, soft bedding, parental smoking, and unsafe sleep environments. Understanding the epidemiology, etiology, and contributory factors is essential for effective prevention and counseling.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity equips clinicians with the knowledge and skills to identify infants at increased risk for SIDS, educate caregivers on safe sleep practices, and implement evidence-based prevention strategies. Participants review SIDS epidemiology, clinical presentation, risk factors, and current recommendations for risk reduction. Emphasis is placed on interprofessional collaboration, engaging pediatricians, nurses, respiratory therapists, and social workers to ensure consistent caregiver education, environmental assessment, and follow-up. Effective team-based coordination enhances early identification of high-risk infants, reinforces adherence to safe sleep guidelines, and supports family-centered interventions to reduce SIDS incidence.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) was defined in 1969 as the sudden, unexpected death of an infant younger than 1 year of age that remains unexplained after a thorough investigation, including review of the medical history, examination of the death scene, and a complete autopsy. [1] [2] By definition, no single cause of death can be identified. SIDS most commonly occurs during sleep and is the leading cause of postneonatal mortality among infants aged 1 to 12 months in the United States.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Introduction
content: The broader term sudden unexpected infant death (SUID)—used to include all sudden, unexpected deaths of infants younger than 1 year old (such as those later attributed to SIDS, accidental suffocation, strangulation in bed, and deaths of unknown cause)—emerged in the early 2000s as clinical and public health practices evolved to improve consistency in death classification and surveillance. SUID covers all sudden and unexpected infant deaths, including those eventually attributed to SIDS, accidental suffocation or asphyxia, and cases where the cause or circumstances remain uncertain. [3] This activity focuses on sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), distinguishing it from other causes of sudden unexpected infant death and emphasizing its distinct epidemiology, risk factors, and prevention strategies. The review examines the epidemiology of SIDS, summarizes current understanding of its etiology, describes the clinical presentation and key risk factors, and highlights evidence-based prevention measures. By consolidating current knowledge, this activity supports healthcare team members in counseling caregivers, identifying infants at increased risk, and promoting adherence to safe sleep practices.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The precise etiology of SIDS remains unknown, but evidence suggests this condition results from an interaction of multiple internal and external factors. The triple-risk model, supported by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), is the most widely accepted explanation, which suggests that SIDS occurs when an infant with an inherent vulnerability, manifested as impaired arousal, cardiorespiratory, or autonomic responses, including inadequate reactions to hypoxemia and hypercarbia, experiences an exogenous trigger during a critical developmental period, usually between 1 and 4 months of age. [4] Internal vulnerabilities include in utero exposures, delayed development, genetic factors, male sex, preterm birth or low birth weight, and abnormalities in brainstem serotonergic neurotransmission.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Exogenous triggers include sleeping prone or on the side, overdressing, airway blockage, and overheating. [4] The risk often multiplies; for instance, prone sleeping in a preterm infant raises the risk more than either factor alone. Supine sleeping remains the most crucial modifiable risk factor, and public health campaigns promoting the "Back to Sleep" position have significantly decreased the SIDS rate. Other hypotheses, such as the bacterial toxin hypothesis, are not endorsed by major professional organizations, although infection may act as a cofactor in some cases. The main view highlights the combination of inherent vulnerability, developmental stage, and environmental stressors as the primary cause framework. [5]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: In the United States, SIDS remains a leading cause of infant mortality. Approximately 3400 cases of SUID occur annually, of which 1400 are diagnosed as SIDS. [6] The SIDS rate has declined dramatically since the early 1990s—from 120 deaths per 100,000 live births in 1992 to 33 per 100,000 in 2019—representing a nearly 75% reduction. However, this progress has plateaued since 2000, and the overall SUID rate has remained relatively constant despite continued public health efforts. SIDS accounted for 1248 deaths in 2019 (37% of all SUIDs) and remains the leading cause of postneonatal mortality (deaths between 28 days and 1 year of age). [4]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Non-Hispanic Black and American Indian/Alaska Native infants have SIDS rates more than twice those of non-Hispanic White infants (0.87 and 0.96 vs 0.42 deaths per 1000 live births, respectively). These disparities persist regardless of socioeconomic status and are present across all SUID categories. [7] SUID rates increased significantly for non-Hispanic Black infants from 2019 to 2020, widening existing disparities. [8]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Globally, SIDS mortality rates decreased by 51% from 1990 to 2019, from approximately 43 to 21 deaths per 100,000 population. However, improvements were disproportionately distributed across regions and sociodemographic index (SDI) levels. Higher SDI and income levels were associated with a lower SIDS burden and greater temporal declines. [9]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Western Europe shows marked between-country variation. From 2005 to 2015, the overall SUID rate was 34.9 per 100,000 live births, decreasing from 40.2 to 29.9. SUID ranked as the second most common cause of death after the neonatal period, though it ranked first in Belgium, Finland, France, and the United Kingdom.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: The SIDS/SUID ratio varied dramatically—from 6.1% in Portugal to 97.8% in Ireland—reflecting differences in diagnostic practices in labeling SUID deaths as SIDS. [10] New Zealand has one of the highest SIDS rates among Western countries, with the rate among Maori natives almost 5 times that of infants of European descent. [7] The incidence of SIDS peaks between 2 and 4 months of age, with approximately 90% of cases occurring before 6 months. Boys are 21% more likely to die of SIDS than girls, and this sex-based disparity has been observed across diverse populations, geographic regions, and time periods. [6] [9] [6] [11] [12]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Following the AAP recommendations and the introduction of public health campaigns promoting supine sleep in 1992, the incidence of SIDS declined substantially in the United States. From 1992 to 2001, the SIDS rate fell from 120 to 56 deaths per 100,000 live births, coinciding with an increase in the proportion of infants placed supine for sleep, from 13% to 72%. According to the AAP, the incidence of SIDS in 2019 was 33 deaths per 100,000 live births in the United States. [4]

Infants with a history of prematurity or prenatal and postnatal smoke exposure are at increased risk of SIDS. [14] [15] [16]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Prematurity is the strongest independent risk factor for SIDS, and the increased risk persists even after the infant reaches their expected due date. [6] Additional epidemiologic associations include rural residence, the presence of older siblings, and a seasonal predominance in winter months. [17] [18] [19] [20] Siblings of infants who died of SIDS have approximately a 4-fold increased risk of SIDS compared with the general population. This familial aggregation likely reflects a combination of shared genetic susceptibility and environmental risk factors, although the relative contributions of each remain uncertain. [21]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: A widely accepted framework for understanding SIDS is the triple-risk model, which proposes that SIDS occurs when an underlying infant vulnerability intersects with a triggering event during a critical developmental period. [22]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Underlying Vulnerability Infants who succumb to SIDS often exhibit impaired physiologic regulatory mechanisms. Post-mortem studies reveal abnormalities in serotonergic signaling within the brainstem, particularly in the arcuate nucleus and other regions that regulate ventilation and blood pressure in response to hypoxia and hypercarbia. [23] [24] Decreased 5-HT1A (the 1A subtype of the serotonin receptor) binding in the medulla has also been observed, potentially disrupting a broad array of autonomic responses mediated by serotonin. [25] Additionally, certain genetic polymorphisms may confer increased susceptibility to SIDS. [26]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Trigger Event The specific triggers that precipitate SIDS remain uncertain. Evidence suggests that prone sleeping increases the risk of suffocation due to decreased arousal, bedding characteristics, and overheating. [27] [28] Prone positioning is associated with longer obstructive events, prolonged sleep duration, and reduced arousal responses. [29] Infants younger than 6 months have a naturally higher arousal threshold, which may exacerbate vulnerability. [27] Cardiac dysfunction has also been implicated as a potential trigger, and infection may play a contributory role: autopsy studies demonstrate that SIDS infants are more frequently colonized or infected with potentially pathogenic organisms than infants dying from other non-infectious causes. [30]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Vulnerable Developmental Stage SIDS most commonly occurs between 2 and 4 months of age, coinciding with the rapid maturation of cardiac, respiratory, and sleep-wake regulatory systems. During this period, infants experience a nadir in blood pressure and demonstrate impaired cardiovascular responses to stress, such as during head-tilt challenges. [31] Sleep architecture and arousal mechanisms also undergo significant developmental maturation during the first 6 months of life, creating a window of heightened susceptibility.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: SIDS has no pathognomonic histopathologic findings, as it is, by definition, a diagnosis of exclusion after thorough investigation reveals no identifiable cause of death. [32] However, several common autopsy findings are frequently observed and may provide clues to underlying mechanisms. Macroscopic findings include petechiae of the thymus, visceral pleura, and epicardium in 68% to 95% of cases, typically more extensive than in non-SIDS deaths.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Pulmonary congestion and edema indicative of terminal left ventricular failure are common, along with oronasal secretions that are frothy, mucoid, and pink or bloody. [33] The lungs are usually well-inflated, arguing against surfactant deficiency. Other typical findings include blood in the heart, prominent lymph nodes, and an empty bladder. [34]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Microscopic examination often reveals minor respiratory tract inflammation, which may contribute to overheating, apnea, or sensitization to bacterial toxins. [34] Intrathoracic petechial hemorrhage is supportive but not obligatory for diagnosis. The thymus typically shows no signs of significant stress, with a normal weight (>15 g) and minimal loss of cortical lymphocytes, supporting that death occurred in an otherwise healthy infant rather than from severe infection or chronic illness. [32]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Neuropathologic findings are the most consistent and pathophysiologically significant abnormalities. Abnormalities of the brainstem serotonergic system occur in up to 70% of SIDS cases, including decreased 5-HT1A receptor binding, reduced serotonin transporter binding, and decreased tissue serotonin levels. [7] Additional findings include delayed neuronal maturation (decreased neuronal nuclear antigen expression), increased dendritic spines, suggesting developmental delay, and increased neuronal apoptosis in the hippocampus and brainstem. [33] Cerebellar abnormalities, including neuronal immaturity, altered apoptosis, and astrogliosis, occur in 62% of sudden infant deaths versus 10% of controls.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Inflammatory markers may be present in SIDS, and elevated interleukin-6 in cerebrospinal fluid has been reported in up to half of infants, at levels similar to those seen in infectious deaths. Occult viral infections, including human parechovirus 3, which primarily affects young infants and can cause systemic or neurologic symptoms, have been detected in the medulla and may trigger localized inflammatory responses; however, their clinical significance remains uncertain. [33]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: SIDS is a postmortem diagnosis of exclusion, and there are no pathognomonic history and physical exam findings. The typical clinical scenario involves an infant aged 21 days to 9 months who is found unresponsive during a sleep period. Infants are often discovered in the morning, with over 80% of deaths occurring between midnight and 6 am. [7] Results from studies suggest that 95% of the SIDS cases were associated with at least one risk factor, and 78% of the cases were associated with at least 2 risk factors, which should be elicited during clinical history-taking and death-scene investigation. [35]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Nonmodifiable risk factors
content: Premature birth Male sex Birth weight below 2500 g Family history of SIDS Siblings of infants who died of SIDS have approximately a 4-fold increased risk of SIDS compared to the general population. However, the absolute risk remains low, with over 99% of subsequent siblings surviving infancy. [21] Young maternal age (less than 20 or 25, depending on the study) This likely serves  as a marker for multiple interconnected risk factors rather than being independently causal, including higher rates of maternal smoking, lower socioeconomic status, reduced prenatal care utilization, unmarried status, and less knowledge about safe sleep practices. However, young maternal age maintains independent predictive value even after adjusting for these variables in multivariate models. [36]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Modifiable risk factors include
content: Sleep environment, including surface sharing, loose bedding, blankets, soft mattresses, crib bumper pads, or sleeping in a car seat or stroller Sleep position, prone or side sleeping versus supine Feeding practices, including breast milk versus formula Tobacco exposure, including maternal smoking during pregnancy and secondhand smoke in the home [6]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Many SIDS deaths occur in unsafe sleep environments, which may act as exogenous stressors in the triple-risk model, including prone or side sleeping, bed sharing, soft bedding, and overheating. [4] [14] SIDS cases typically show minimal specific physical examination findings, with the diagnosis requiring exclusion of other causes through comprehensive death scene investigation and autopsy. The most characteristic findings are nonspecific markers of sudden death rather than pathognomonic features. Physical examination findings at the death scene may include: Frothy fluid escaping from the nose and mouth [34] [37] Postmortem gravity-dependent pooling of blood after death, producing skin discoloration that helps determine the infant's position at the time of death and whether the body was moved Absence of trauma or signs of suffocation, such as facial petechiae When present, this raises the question of intentional or accidental suffocation or child maltreatment.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: SIDS is a diagnosis of exclusion with no pathognomonic clinical, laboratory, or pathologic findings. The evaluation requires a comprehensive and standardized investigation with 3 essential components: a review of the infant's clinical history, a thorough death scene investigation with caregiver interviews and doll reenactment, and a complete autopsy with ancillary testing. [32] This systematic approach is necessary to exclude accidental suffocation, trauma, infection, metabolic disease, and other identifiable causes of sudden infant death.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Clinical History
content: The clinical history should be reviewed early in the evaluation and includes prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal medical records, growth and developmental history, prior illnesses, and family history. Interviews with caregivers should be conducted by culturally competent professionals using nonaccusatory, open-ended questions to elicit information on sleep position, soft bedding, the sleep environment, co-sleeping, recent respiratory symptoms, feeding practices, tobacco exposure, and prenatal care. Because there is no biological marker that conclusively distinguishes SIDS from accidental suffocation, information obtained from the history and witnessed accounts is critical in efforts to determine the cause of death. [32]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Death Scene Investigation
content: Death scene investigation is a cornerstone of the evaluation. The AAP recommends that investigations follow standardized protocols, such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Sudden Unexplained Infant Death Investigation Reporting Form. Scene investigation should include caregiver and witness interviews, detailed narrative documentation of the circumstances surrounding the death, and doll reenactment to reconstruct infant positioning and identify potential environmental hazards. Photographic documentation of the sleep environment is essential. This should include the condition of the crib or bed, the sleep surface, bedding, and the presence of soft or loose objects. Additional documentation includes room temperature, overall environmental conditions, and the reactions of the infant's caregivers. [32] [38]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Death Scene Investigation
content: Data from the SUID Case Registry demonstrated that 98% of 770 sudden unexplained infant deaths underwent a death scene investigation, with narrative descriptions completed in 90% and witness interviews in 88%. [39] Scene investigation findings are critical, as the absence of evidence for accidental death, mechanical asphyxia, suffocation, wedging, or entrapment characterizes classic SIDS. [34] However, many deaths occur in unsafe sleep environments—such as prone or side positioning, soft bedding, bed sharing, or overheating—which represent exogenous stressors in the triple-risk model. [4]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Autopsy and Metabolic Screening
content: A complete autopsy is mandatory and should be performed as soon as feasible, ideally within 24 hours of death. Autopsy identifies a definitive cause of death in only approximately 15% of deaths initially suspected to be SIDS. [34] The examination should include comprehensive external and internal evaluations of all major organs and tissues, including the brain; a complete histologic examination; comprehensive toxicology testing; complete radiographs and a skeletal survey; microbiologic testing; and metabolic screening studies. [32] [39]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Autopsy and Metabolic Screening
content: In the SUID Case Registry, all 770 infants underwent autopsy, with histology, microbiology, and other pathology completed in 98% of cases and toxicology in 97%. [39] Recommended metabolic screening includes plasma acylcarnitine profile, quantitative plasma carnitine levels, quantitative plasma amino acid analysis, qualitative urine organic acid analysis, and plasma lactate and pyruvate levels. [32] The autopsy should specifically confirm and document the absence of potentially fatal pathologic findings, including any evidence of trauma, abuse, neglect, or unintentional injury that could explain the death. Findings that may be present but are not diagnostic include intrathoracic petechial hemorrhages (particularly subserosal thymic petechiae) and minor inflammatory infiltrates in the respiratory tract.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Evaluation -- Autopsy and Metabolic Screening
content: There should be no evidence of substantial thymic stress effect, such as thymic weight less than 15 g or moderate to severe cortical lymphocyte depletion. [32] Assessment for panlobular microvesicular fatty change in the liver is essential, as its presence prompts further evaluation for inherited metabolic disorders. [34] The diagnosis of SIDS is supported when a sudden, unexplained death occurs during sleep in an infant within the typical age range and the evaluation—including clinical history, death scene investigation, autopsy, toxicology, microbiology, radiology, vitreous chemistry, and metabolic testing—fails to identify an alternative cause.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Because SIDS is a postmortem diagnosis, there is no medical treatment or acute management for the infant. When SIDS is suspected, a comprehensive investigation is required to exclude alternative causes of death. Management is primarily supportive and focused on the family. All members of the medical team should provide compassionate care, reassurance, and clear education about SIDS and the investigative process. If a genetic etiology or inherited condition is identified during evaluation, referral for genetic counseling is appropriate. Families may also benefit from bereavement counseling.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Many conditions may mimic SIDS, including child maltreatment, accidental suffocation, metabolic disorders, infections, and congenital malformations. Among these, fatal child abuse and metabolic disease deserve particular attention because they may affect other family members. The differential diagnosis of SIDS includes the following.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis -- Accidental suffocation and strangulation
content: Suffocation represents the most commonly encountered cause of sleep-related infant death, accounting for 14% of SUID cases. Mechanisms include soft bedding obstruction (69% of suffocation deaths), overlay by another person (19%), and wedging/entrapment between objects (12%). Soft-bedding deaths occur most often in adult beds (49%) with infants in a prone position (82%), frequently with blankets obstructing the airway. Overlay deaths typically occur in adult beds (71%), with the adult caregiver overlaying the infant (47%). Wedging deaths most commonly involve entrapment between the mattress and the wall (48%). Among explained and possible suffocation deaths, approximately 75% result from airway obstruction attributed to soft bedding. [14] [40]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis -- Nonaccidental trauma
content: Fatal child abuse or neglect can mimic or be misclassified as SIDS on initial evaluation. [41] This can be distinguished from SIDS by a combination of historical inconsistencies, death scene findings, and investigative results that are not characteristic of an unexplained natural death. Concerning features include discrepancies between the caregiver's account and the infant's developmental abilities or injuries, a history of prior unexplained injuries or previous involvement with child protective services, delays in seeking medical care, or differing narratives from multiple caregivers. Scene investigation may reveal an unsafe or altered environment inconsistent with reported events, evidence of smothering or overlaying, or signs of neglect. Autopsy findings that argue against SIDS include unexplained fractures (especially rib or metaphyseal fractures), intracranial hemorrhage without an adequate accidental mechanism, visceral injuries, bruising, or evidence of prior injuries.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis -- Cardiac conduction abnormalities
content: Cardiac channelopathies (eg, long QT syndrome and other ion channel defects) can cause sudden cardiac arrest in infancy and may be discovered on postmortem molecular autopsy or family testing. Fatal cardiac dysrhythmias may cause approximately 10% of deaths previously attributed to SIDS. Postmortem genetic testing for cardiac channelopathy panels should be considered, particularly when the family history is positive or when there are recurrent deaths in the family. [42] [43] [44]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis -- Inborn errors of metabolism
content: Clinical features suggestive of an underlying metabolic disorder include the unexpected death of a sibling, a family history of sudden unexpected events such as a brief resolved unexplained event, Reye syndrome, or myopathy, and pre-mortem signs or symptoms such as poor weight gain, lethargy, recurrent vomiting, hypoglycemia, hypotonia, hyperventilation, serious infections, or elevated aminotransferase levels. Metabolic defects may involve the metabolism of fatty acids, branched-chain amino acids, urea cycle products, or mitochondrial dysfunction. The most common metabolic conditions causing sudden death in infancy are fatty acid oxidation disorders, particularly medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. [45] [46] Other inborn errors of metabolism, including urea cycle defects, organic acidemias, and amino acid metabolism disorders, can present with acute metabolic encephalopathy in young infants. These disorders may lead to sudden death, especially during periods of metabolic stress, and can often be detected by newborn screening or specialized postmortem metabolic testing. [47] [48]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis -- Infection
content: Bacterial sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis, bronchiolitis, and other systemic or central nervous system infections can present with sudden deterioration and death. Neonates with sepsis may show nonspecific signs, including temperature instability, hypotension, poor perfusion, metabolic acidosis, apnea, respiratory distress, lethargy, seizures, and feeding intolerance. Initial symptoms may be minimal, such as apnea alone or tachypnea with retractions. [49]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Clinicians should rule out these differential diagnoses using a combination of history, death-scene investigation, autopsy, radiographic evaluation, and specialized laboratory testing. Careful exclusion of alternative diagnoses is essential before assigning a diagnosis of SIDS.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Despite a widespread campaign promoting the supine sleep position for infants, adherence to this practice in the United States peaked at approximately 80% in 2015. Compliance never reached the target level. [50] In a 2019 United States survey, 93% of parents reported hearing from clinicians about placing the baby in a supine position for sleep, yet only 78% reported adhering to the recommendation. [51] Furthermore, parents were less likely to recall hearing about other safe sleeping practices, including avoiding soft objects near the bed (85%), using a safe sleep surface (84%), and room-sharing without bed-sharing (50%).

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Safe sleep practices are central to reducing the risk of SIDS. The AAP recommends that all infants be placed on their backs for every sleep on a firm, flat, noninclined surface in the caregiver's room, on a separate sleep surface, ideally for at least the first 6 months. Room sharing without bed sharing reduces the risk of SIDS, suffocation, strangulation, and entrapment by as much as 50%. The sleep environment should be free of soft objects, pillows, blankets, comforters, mattress toppers, plush fabrics, stuffed toys, or loose bedding. Bed elevation and inclined sleep surfaces are not recommended, as they do not prevent gastroesophageal reflux and may increase the risk of airway compromise. [6] [14]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Infants who can roll independently from supine to prone and back may remain in the position they assume. Still, evidence supports maintaining supine positioning at the start of sleep until age 1. Swaddling is safe only when the infant is placed supine with adequate room for the hips and knees, and should be discontinued once the infant attempts to roll (typically at 3–4 months). [14]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Breast milk feeding, whether directly or with expressed milk, reduces the risk of SIDS, with the greatest protection observed with exclusive and longer-duration of feeding. Any consumption of breast milk offers some protection against SIDS. [6] [52] Caregivers should be encouraged to provide human milk whenever possible. Some parents may be unable or choose not to breastfeed. Clinicians should discuss feeding practices respectfully and without judgment, and families who do not breastfeed should still be counseled on all other safe sleep recommendations. [14]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Routine recommended immunizations are also associated with a reduced risk of SIDS. [14] Pacifier use at naps and bedtime reduces SIDS risk, even if the pacifier falls out during sleep. Infants who refuse a pacifier should not be forced to accept it; however, offering it again later is appropriate. Caregivers should introduce pacifiers after breastfeeding is firmly established. [14]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Avoiding exposure to smoke, nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, opioids, and illicit drugs during pregnancy and after birth is critical. Bed sharing with smokers is particularly hazardous. The risk of SIDS is particularly high when the infant shares a bed with an adult smoker, even when the adult does not smoke in bed. Electronic cigarettes contain nicotine, which may also increase risk. [14] [53] Because home cardiorespiratory monitors have not been shown to prevent SIDS and may foster caregiver complacency, they are not recommended for routine use. [14] [54]

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Families with infants at higher baseline risk, such as preterm infants or those with a history of SIDS in a sibling, should receive especially careful counseling. Clinicians, hospital staff, and childcare providers should consistently promote safe sleep practices, beginning in pregnancy and continuing at well-child visits for all families during the first year. Media, including advertising, TV, and movies, should model safe sleep practices, and manufacturers should adhere to these guidelines when designing infant products. Campaigns such as theNational Institute of Child Health and Human Development's "Safe to Sleep" remain essential for promoting safe sleep habits as the social norm.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes -- Teaching and Prevention
content: The healthcare team plays a critical role in preventing SIDS through education, modeling, and institutional policies. Hospitals and nurseries should establish and maintain written policies on safe sleep practices, including supine positioning on a firm, flat sleep surface, avoidance of soft bedding, and room-sharing without bed-sharing. Staff should model these behaviors for parents, explain the rationale for the recommendations, and reinforce the importance of following them.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes -- Teaching and Prevention
content: Clinicians should provide culturally sensitive counseling, acknowledging potential barriers such as financial constraints, cultural norms, concerns about infant comfort, or logistical challenges, while consistently emphasizing the benefits of a safe sleep environment. Epidemiologic studies have demonstrated that prone sleeping is a major preventable risk factor for SIDS. Public health campaigns in the 1990s and 2000s promoting supine sleep have significantly reduced SIDS incidence, though deaths continue to occur. Physicians, other clinicians, and nurses should continue to educate parents and caregivers about SIDS risks and safe sleep practices during routine health maintenance visits in the first year. All state regulatory agencies should require that child care providers receive education on safe infant sleep and implement written policies for safe sleep in child care settings.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes -- After SIDS Occurs
content: When an infant dies unexpectedly, coordinated care from the healthcare team and emergency responders is essential. Emergency responders should be trained to: Observe and document the death scene carefully. Provide emotional support to caregivers, allowing families to hold the child if they wish. Understand grief responses and the cultural practices of the families in their community.

title: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes -- After SIDS Occurs
content: In the emergency department, personnel should provide sensitive, unhurried support to families, explaining the rationale for the autopsy and death scene investigation, including transportation arrangements and timing. If families arrive in a private vehicle, law enforcement should be contacted to secure the area and identify witnesses. Hospital staff should assist with transportation home, confirm contact information, provide referrals to bereavement or SIDS/SUIDS programs, guide families regarding funeral arrangements, and recommend hospital and community contacts for future questions and concerns. The healthcare team, including physicians, nurses, and nursery staff, should ensure consistent messaging and compassionate care, reinforcing safe sleep recommendations and addressing families' emotional needs. Clear institutional policies and staff training on both prevention and post-event care help standardize responses, minimize family distress, and improve overall team outcomes.
